title: IBM’s ‘true ROI’ comment hits shares, exposing ETF risks
detail:
IBM’s ‘true ROI’ comment hits shares, exposing ETF risks
Opeyemi Babalola
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 11:33 AM PDT 6 min read
IBM
Trade IBM on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Plenty of investors own International Business Machines Corp. (IBM) without ever buying a share. The 115-year-old company sits near the top of several tech dividend, Dow dividend and even quantum computing funds.

That hidden exposure got tested on Thursday, October 22, 2026. IBM beat Wall Street's third-quarter estimates, yet its shares fell about 7% in morning trading, according to 24/7 Wall St. The trigger was not the numbers but one remark about how customers judge their AI bills.

On the earnings call, CEO Arvind Krishna said big enterprises now weigh the "true ROI" of their AI spending. He added that some worry the spending could run out of control without a real payoff. Investors heard customers reaching for the brakes.

Also read: IBM spent $11 billion on growth as its own software stalls

Those nerves trace back to July, when IBM suffered the worst single-day drop in its history, falling about 25%. Big deals slipped, and analysts said clients were redirecting budgets elsewhere, including servers and memory.

A handful of funds carry most of the IBM risk

About 557 ETFs hold IBM, according to Seeking Alpha, but most own only a sliver. The real exposure sits in a short list of income and quantum funds.

The First Trust NASDAQ Technology Dividend Index Fund (TDIV) had 8.65% of its assets in IBM as of October 21, according to First Trust. At that weight, a 7% slide in IBM trims roughly six-tenths of a point from the fund if nothing else moves. That stings, but it does not break a portfolio.

Quantum funds are the stranger case. The WisdomTree Quantum Computing Fund (WQTM) and Corgi Quantum Computing ETF (CQTM) both list IBM in their top 10, according to WisdomTree and Investing.com. People bought those funds for a moonshot, and on Thursday, they got a lesson in corporate IT budgets instead.

I think that overlap is the exposure most fund owners miss. A dividend ETF and a quantum ETF can quietly stack up a large IBM position, and both just reacted to the same sentence.

Fund owners can run these checks before reacting

Start with the fund's own holdings page, since weights move daily and lists differ by source. TDIV also rebalances quarterly and caps single stocks, according to its prospectus, so an outsized IBM weight gets trimmed on schedule.

Then weigh concentration. The Vanguard High Dividend Yield ETF (VYM) had under 1% in IBM, which means less risk and a smaller rebound.

None of this calls for a quick trade. It does depend on what Krishna's sentence actually meant.

title: Should You Buy Hewlett Packard Enterprise Stock For Its Cash?
detail:
Should You Buy Hewlett Packard Enterprise Stock For Its Cash?
Trefis Team
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 1:42 PM PDT 4 min read
HPE
DELL
IBM
CSCO
SMCI
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) produced free cash flow equal to 5.6% of its market value over the past year, against 4.3% for the median S&P 500 company. A yield that high marks either a business on sale or one the market expects to shrink, and the price appears to assume HPE's server and networking sales will not keep producing this much cash. So how much of that cash can you count on?

HPE's Cash Is At A Three-Year High

HPE has produced free cash in every twelve-month period since mid-2023, but only the past year brought this much. The total reached $4.16 billion, against $0.225 billion in the twelve months before. After lenders are served, that cash belongs to owners whether or not HPE pays it out. If the market comes to give that cash more credit, the share price could rise to reflect it.

The cash comes from a bigger business. Revenue reached $41.9 billion over the past year, up 26.6%. That period includes the Juniper Networks business HPE bought. In the latest quarter, management said orders were led by demand in traditional servers, AI systems, and networking. HPE spent 37.9% of the cash its operations brought in on capital spending.

Part of the cash must serve lenders first. HPE's debt minus its cash came to $14.0 billion at the end of July 2026, or 18.9% of its market value. Against market value plus that debt, the yield is 4.7%. After selling its Telco Solutions business, management said on its September 2, 2026 call that it would retire $1.25 billion of notes maturing that month.

Management Expects Thinner Margins As AI Sales Grow

HPE already earns a thin profit on each sale. Its operating margin was 7.8% over the past year, against 18.5% for the S&P 500 taken as one company. That margin has risen from 6.2% the year before.

Management expects some near-term pressure on that profit. On its September 2 call, management said gross margin should move back toward historical levels as AI systems grow and traditional server prices normalize, and the operating margin should fall in fiscal Q4 2026 on a higher mix of AI systems and on pricing. Both are forecasts, not reported falls. Shortages of parts, DDR5 among them, have also limited how many traditional servers HPE can ship, management said.

Management is working on margins and supply. It expects $600 million a year of savings from the Juniper Networks acquisition by the end of fiscal 2028, and the company is seeking multiyear supply agreements with its partners. It also raised its fiscal 2027 revenue growth forecast to 15% at the midpoint, from 10%. So the doubt is about how much HPE keeps from each sale, not about a business that is shrinking.

title: IBM's Software Growth Sped Up and Its Stock Barely Moved. I'd Start Buying.
detail:
IBM's Software Growth Sped Up and Its Stock Barely Moved. I'd Start Buying.
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 1:01 AM PDT 5 min read
IBM
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Before International Business Machines (NYSE:IBM) posted third-quarter results on Oct. 21, I set a bar for buying the stock. I wanted software revenue growth back in the high single digits and recurring revenue rising close to 10%.

The software half of that test came through. IBM's software segment reported 9% year-over-year revenue growth at constant currency (a measure that strips out exchange-rate moves). In the second quarter, it grew just 5%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

But shares barely budged on Thursday, the day after the report, closing up less than 1% after falling as much as 4% during the session. IBM stock closed at $252.11, which puts it about 23% under the $329.23 record close it set on June 2.

In September, I wrote that I expected IBM stock to be higher in five years but still wouldn't buy it. What I was waiting for was software growth that picked back up. I think this quarter delivered it.

Image source: Getty Images.

Software is growing faster again

Software matters more to IBM's profits than any other piece of the business. The segment made up around 46% of third-quarter revenue but about 65% of the company's segment profit, so its swing this year counts for a lot.

Software's constant-currency growth was 8% in the first quarter of 2026. It cooled to 5% in the second quarter before jumping to 9% in the third -- its fastest rate of the year. Transaction processing, the software linked largely to IBM's mainframes, did most of the swinging. It dropped 9% at constant currency in the second quarter and climbed 10% in the third. Better still, software's segment profit rose 15% year over year to around $2.7 billion, and its margin widened to 35% from 33%.

"Software revenue growth accelerated four points sequentially to 9% this quarter, including over four points of organic growth," chief financial officer Jim Kavanaugh said on IBM's Oct. 21 earnings call.

Granted, some of the jump is timing. Kavanaugh said around a quarter of the acceleration came from big deals that slipped out of the second quarter and closed in the third. The other three-quarters, he said, came from new business.

I think this makes the second quarter look like the exception, not the start of a slide.

Does the unchanged revenue forecast matter?

IBM still expects full-year revenue to climb 4% to 5% at constant currency, the same range it set in July. But it now expects 2026 free cash flow to rise by over $1 billion from last year's $14.7 billion. In July, it expected a gain of around $1 billion.

Accenture (ACN) stock returned 77.4% over the three months to October 22, 2026, against 3.7% for the S&P 500. Such a run leaves shareholders with more to lose, and one remark from the October 1 earnings call merits their attention: management discussed what Accenture can charge its clients. So what did management say about prices, and how much of Accenture's revenue is at stake?

Accenture Saw Lower Pricing In Many Areas

Management said on the October 1 call that Accenture saw lower pricing in many areas of its business in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, which ended August 31. Pricing was overall stable for the full year, and management described the market as highly competitive. So the shift is a recent, one-quarter development rather than a yearlong trend.

Management also discussed AI on the call. Accenture is delivering more AI efficiencies to clients, management said, and has more than made up for that with new kinds of work and broader scope.

Hiring patterns reflect the same shift. Revenue per person rose in fiscal 2026, and management expects to hire at a lower rate in fiscal 2027, in part due to AI. That outlines the threat in plain terms: if AI lets Accenture do the same work with fewer people, clients may expect to pay less for it, and so far management has found new work to fill the gap.

How Much Of Accenture's Revenue Is Exposed?

Management did not say how much revenue saw lower pricing. The pressure applies to a business with $74.2 billion in revenue over the twelve months ended August 31, 2026, up 6.5% in U.S. dollars from a year earlier. Consulting revenues were $36.9 billion in fiscal 2026, up 3% in local currency, the slower of the two halves of that revenue. Managed services revenues, derived from running applications, infrastructure and operations for clients, were $37.3 billion, up 6% in local currency.

The company's outlook leaves room for a weaker year. Management expects fiscal 2027 revenue to grow 3% to 6% in local currency, against 5% in fiscal 2026, and expects acquisitions to add 2% to 2.5% of that. The bottom of the range allows for deterioration, management said.

The share price leaves less room than it did in the summer. On June 30, 2026, the stock traded at 9.8 times earnings, its lowest multiple at any of the 40 quarter ends since fiscal 2017. It now trades at 18.6 times earnings, against 23.0 for the S&P 500, and its latest close was 7.7% below its highest close of the past year. The current price appears to assume that lower pricing stays contained.
